content.comment_body: Hello, I recently switched to a new notebook and set up a fresh installation of [product_name] V8 since I need to maintain several previous projects created with [product_name] hardware. My old notebook stopped working and I previously used [product_name] V6 on it. After installing everything as instructed, I tried connecting to the hardware using my regular serial cable, but received an error stating: "Unable to access the IP Address COM5" (COM5 is my USB-to-Serial adapter's port). I also tested on a desktop PC with a dedicated serial port, chose serial cable connection, and got the same error (though on COM3 instead of COM6). Is there something I am missing? This should be a simple task, but I cannot get the software to connect via serial cable. By the way, I've worked with modules marked [article_no] and [article_no]. Thank you for any advice.
Here’s a screenshot showing the error message I encounter:
You likely need to install the proper USB cable driver. Is your new computer running a different operating system? [product_name] V8 supports up to Windows 8. Hope this helps.

Thanks for replying. Both notebooks use Windows 7 64-bit. Previously I had [product_name] V6, now I’ve installed V8 (I couldn’t install the old version due to missing files). The old V6 did not support ethernet, so serial was the only choice. I doubt it’s the USB-serial adapter issue since the same error occurred on a desktop PC using a physical RS232 port (no adapter). I searched online and saw claims about setting the interface under TOOLS-OPTIONS, but I don’t see any such setting in V8.0.0.

You’re correct: In [product_name] V8, interface selection isn’t located in Tools. If you press upload/download, you can select the cable type at the top left of the dialog and the COM port at the top right. I still think the issue may be with the USB driver. If you have the original V8 DVD, the Win64 driver should be included. Installing an older version and then updating to V8 may not update the USB driver, so manual installation might be needed. You can find the necessary driver online. USB-to-Serial converters have caused many issues in the past; ideally, use direct USB-Ethernet adapters for newer hardware. Also, ensure you’ve chosen the correct hardware in the software – otherwise, errors will persist. Hope this helps.

Thanks for your insight. I suspected the USB driver too, so I tested with a desktop PC with a direct RS232 port (no USB involved) and still got the same error. The error message itself is odd: "Unable to access IP address COM3" – it simultaneously mentions an IP address and a COM port, which seems illogical.

If you haven't completely removed the old software, it may remain and interfere. New installations might not uninstall previous versions. Also check that your Java runtime is updated and matches your PC's specifications.

There is no leftover software since V6 was only installed on my old notebook which is now unusable. Both my new notebook and desktop have no previous installations of [product_name]. I purchased an original V8 release from an authorized source. Both computers are running the latest Java version.
I have the same problem and have tried everything I can think of. I installed the USB driver, checked it in Control Panel and it works, but the issue persists. Can anyone help?

I have a laptop with Windows 7 (64-bit) and [product_name] V8 installed. The hardware RS232 cable is connected to COM1. On most PCs, RS232 is COM1 or COM2. I select it in the interface dialog and test; everything works – I can upload/download from/to my hardware. I also tested a USB programming cable: connected to PC, selected cable and port (COM1, COM3, or COM10), and it worked. So: with a direct RS232 cable, COM1/COM2 should work, and with a USB cable, select the USB-assigned COM port. I use no additional converters – just a docking station. Hope this is useful.

Thank you for explaining. I realize it works for you and others, but for me and a few others, V8 isn't working. Whether I use a USB adapter or not, the error message stays the same – and the error text itself isn’t very logical.

Are you still experiencing this? What do your Windows Device settings show? Any non-standard software installed that manages virtual serial ports? If nothing works, perhaps you should contact [company_name] Support directly.

I installed the software on my notebook and tested on a desktop – same errors both times. On the desktop the RS232 port was native, no virtual driver involved. The error “Unable to access the IP Address COM2” (or COM5/COM6 on the notebook) makes little sense since IP addresses shouldn’t mix with COM port identifiers. Not sure where to seek support besides this forum.

I cannot directly solve your issue, but here’s how to reach [company_name] Support: [url] – Look for "my request" shortcut on the left under your profile name (highlighted in the example image). Please share any outcomes with us. Good luck!
Thank you very much! I'm submitting a support request now and will post updates once I receive a response.

I forgot: There's a specific installation sequence for [product_name] and the USB cable. You must install the software and driver before plugging the USB cable into your PC, otherwise it may not function correctly. To reset: Uninstall the USB driver from Device Manager, then connect the cable and remove it from the interfaces (COM & LPT). Right-click and uninstall. Then uninstall [product_name], restart, and re-install everything as administrator for all users. Keep the USB cable unplugged while installing, following the instructions provided with the cable. After software installation, connect everything and retry. Also, what USB version are you using – 2.0 or 3.0? The programming cable is typically designed for USB 2.0. Hope this helps.
A new question from [user_name] has been moved to a separate thread titled 'Cable for [product_name] PROM'. Best regards, [user_name]

Thanks again for your help. I did the installation with the cable unplugged and tried with a desktop (no USB, just RS232) and got the same result. I submitted a support request and got an email with a PDF containing instructions from the manual about ethernet connections – even though my request never mentioned ethernet as my hardware lacks an ethernet port. Seems tech support didn’t read the details. Anyway, thank you for your support.

[Off topic] Unfortunately that’s my one critique with support – the first step is showing documentation. Some users may give up or find answers here. Stay calm, thank them for their efforts, and politely ask for a closer look at your issue while adding screenshots. With thorough follow-up, detailed troubleshooting often begins. Hang in there and good luck!
Oops! I think I let my frustration show when speaking with support. I’ll try to stay polite, as you suggest.

Someone told me USB 3.0 ports are usually blue, black ones are USB 2.0. My laptop has two blue USB ports, so they should be 3.0, and Device Manager confirms Intel USB3.0. Both ports work well with my USB programming cable and hardware version 6. To connect: upload from hardware to PC, select the cable and try each COM port in the list; one should work. For downloads, you need to check other settings in the software (E-Stand and hardware version). Hope this helps.

[Off topic] It’s important to remember everyone is human, including support reps. Apologize if needed to clear any misunderstandings – they are just following company guidelines. And if service quality is poor, always use the feedback form after your case.

I use a serial cable for the hardware and a USB/RS232 adapter from Digitus, released for USB 2.0 but it also works with USB 3.0. It creates virtual COM4, visible in Device Manager when plugged in, and I can connect to my old [article_no] module via COM4 without trouble.

Most users don’t have issues connecting via Serial Cable to these controllers. There’s likely some minor detail in my installation causing trouble. I recovered my old notebook’s hard drive and set up a virtual machine using the data. With that, I was able to use my previous [product_name] V6 setup and access the hardware. For now, this is my workaround, though I’m limited to old software features. Still hoping to get V8 working and will update here if I do. Thanks to everyone for their assistance.

Hi! [user_name], I have the same problem with my controller. When I attempt to transfer a program from controller to PC, I get 'Unable to access IP address COM14 (13,12...)'. I’ve tried all the suggestions above and searched online, but nothing worked. I tried with an older V5.0, same issue. Possibly it’s caused by an outdated cable with USB adapter. I haven’t tried a new cable, and I’m not sure where the issue is.
I think the problem is the USB adapter. I use two [product_name] [article_no] and an old [article_no] with a serial cable for data transfer.

For me, the issue appeared both on a notebook using a USB-RS232 adapter and on a desktop PC using a direct RS232 port with NO adapter. So the root problem may be somewhere else, since it happens even on systems with built-in serial ports.
Did you try using a different cable? Or using a different controller?

Yes, I tried with two cables and two different controllers. As mentioned earlier, I was able to create a virtual machine from my old notebook’s drive to use my old V6 software and repair the hardware since V8 wouldn’t work.
A new question from [user_name] was moved to a separate discussion titled "Unable to access the IP Address COM1". Best regards, [user_name]

Hello, I encountered the same problem with an old module [article_no] and solved it. There’s a third option in the Card menu: PC to Controller. No problems with my old [article_no]. Best greetings, [user_name]

I had the same error 'Unable to access the IP Address COM3' when using the cable. The message is unclear as no IP protocol is involved when using a serial cable. I use [product_name] Control 8.2.1 on Windows 10. Changing the COM port fixed it: In Device Manager, under Ports, find Silicon Labs CP210x USB to UART Bridge (e.g., COM3), then advanced settings to change the port number to COM1. A restart of the software was required for the correct port to be recognized. Hope this helps.
I have exactly the same issue. Tried all of the above, but nothing works. I have the [article_no], Windows 7 64-bit, and the cable uses a U232-P9 converter. Is there a solution?
Is your hardware actually a 25-year-old [product_name] or do you have a new '[article_no]'?
Yes, it's 25 years old.

You need an old RS232 cable for [product_name] with a RS232-to-USB converter if your PC doesn’t have a RS232 port. The best models use the FTDI chipset – that’s what I use. Alternatively, a USB cable can work, but non-original ones (e.g., unbranded versions) may cause trouble.
I have that converter, followed all instructions above, and it's still not working.
Not familiar with that converter or its chipset. I use a Digitus converter with FTDI chipset, which works on Windows XP SP3 and Windows 7 without problems for me.
Hello again! Is this the correct converter? [url] If so, do you know where to purchase it?
Yes, that’s the correct model. On Windows 7, it works without issues – no driver installation required, as the OS recognizes it automatically.

Very old [product_name] models need to be switched to PC-Controller programming mode. Based on my knowledge, it doesn’t matter if you use the original RS232 or USB programming cable. Nowadays, USB programming cables are preferred since most PCs/laptops lack serial ports. Converters often cause trouble, especially after OS upgrades. To find the right COM port: disconnect the cable/converter, access Device Manager (COM & LPT section), then plug in the cable/converter and check for the new COM port entry. If that port isn’t selectable in the software, try a different USB port. Never use programming cables/converters on a USB hub; the COM port number may change depending on the port. As a last resort, install USB cable drivers manually. Hope this helps.
Everything is now working. With very old [product_name], switching to PC-Controller programming mode is required. Thanks.
Please write future posts in English for clarity.

I had the same issue. What resolved it was updating from [product_name] Soft Comfort 8.3.0 to 8.3.1, available here: [url] My PLC: [article_no], USB Cable: [article_no], USB cable driver: version 11.2.0.167 from [url]. OS: Windows 11 PRO.

Switching from COM3 to COM1 would probably solve it for me too. Unfortunately, my PC reserves COM1 for another function, so I’m now using a different laptop with a free COM1 port. This new laptop had the same problem; changing the driver’s port from COM5 to COM1 in Device Manager and rebooting fixed it. Now I have to bring two computers with me!

analysis.insight_summary: Forum users struggle with serial connectivity between [product_name] hardware and [product_name] V8 software, especially when error messages incorrectly reference both IP addresses and COM ports. The confusion stems from legacy serial communication overlap with modern network features, inconsistent error messages, and USB driver hassles. Attempts to resolve the issue include testing various cables/adapters, switching COM ports, and reinstalling drivers. Success varies, often depending on precise hardware combinations, correct interface selection in the software, and sometimes using older setups or different computers as workarounds.
analysis.user_expectations: Users hope for seamless ongoing support for legacy serial communications in the latest software versions, clear connection setup options, straightforward error messages, and reliable troubleshooting resources. They expect accurate documentation and responsive support when facing persistent issues with standard hardware and drivers.
